Western crowned pigeon (Goura cristata) chicks hatch from a single egg after an incubation period of 28.5 days [ab = 28.5 days] when the nest is maintained at a temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], a thermal condition typical of the lowland rainforest floor where these birds nest. At hatching, the altricial nestling weighs approximately 49.8 grams [Ww0 = approximately 49.8 grams], a relatively modest mass for a bird that will eventually reach a substantial adult size. This initial weight reflects the yolk-dependent embryo's reliance on endogenous reserves prior to the onset of parental provisioning. Field observations indicate that the chick, initially blind and nearly naked, is brooded intensively by both parents during the first week post-hatching. The rapid growth trajectory of the nestling is supported by a diet of regurgitated fruit pulp and invertebrates, a pattern common among Columbidae. Daily weighing of captive-reared individuals confirms that mass gain is consistent and predictable, with the chick doubling its hatch weight within the first ten days under optimal conditions.

Throughout the developmental period, the young bird undergoes a series of physiological and morphological changes that culminate in fledging. Flight feather maturation proceeds steadily, and the chick achieves its first flight at approximately 33 days after hatching [tx = approximately 33 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions typical of this species' active metabolic range, specifically 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This milestone, marking the transition from nestling to fledgling, is comparatively rapid for a bird of this body size and reflects the selective pressures of a predator-rich environment where early mobility offers a survival advantage. The fledgling, still dependent on parental feeding for several weeks thereafter, begins to explore surrounding branches and the forest floor, gradually improving its foraging efficiency on fallen fruits and seeds. Post-fledging survival appears closely tied to the availability of food resources in the territory, which is defended year-round by the monogamous pair.

Sexual maturation in the Western crowned pigeon is a protracted process relative to many smaller columbids. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal development and the emergence of adult plumage characteristics, is reached at 99 days after hatching [tp = 99 days after hatching] at an ambient temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This timing, however, does not immediately translate into reproductive activity; the species exhibits a notable delay between physiological maturity and the first breeding attempt. The attainment of full adult body mass and the establishment of a stable territory appear to be prerequisites for successful reproduction. Adult females ultimately reach an asymptotic mass of up to 2400 grams [Wwi = up to 2400 grams], with a typical range spanning from 1800 to 2400 grams, making this one of the largest pigeon species globally. This substantial body size is accompanied by a relatively slow life-history pace.

The first breeding event in the Western crowned pigeon occurs considerably later than the onset of puberty, reflecting the time required to secure a high-quality territory and establish a pair bond. The age at first successful reproduction has been documented at 3.1 years after hatching [tR = 3.1 years after hatching] under the thermal conditions typical of its active metabolic period at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This delayed first brood is characteristic of large-bodied, long-lived birds that invest heavily in offspring care. Under optimal conditions, the maximum reproductive rate is limited to a single egg per year [Ri = single egg per year], expressed as a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and only one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. The extended parental care period, which includes both brooding and post-fledging provisioning, likely constrains the capacity for more frequent nesting attempts. This life-history strategy aligns with that of other large island-endemic columbids.

Lifespan data for the Western crowned pigeon suggest that individuals can achieve considerable longevity, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 24.7 years [am = approximately 24.7 years] when maintained at the species' preferred thermal regime of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This extended lifespan is consistent with the species' low reproductive rate and delayed maturity, forming a classic slow life-history syndrome. Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained through respirometry trials have recorded a maximum oxygen consumption of 768 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 768 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], a value that reflects the metabolic demands of a large, ground-foraging bird inhabiting a warm, humid tropical environment. These physiological and demographic parameters underscore the species' vulnerability to anthropogenic pressures, including habitat loss and hunting, as the combination of low fecundity and high adult survival makes population recovery from declines exceptionally slow. Conservation efforts must therefore prioritize the protection of breeding adults and their lowland forest habitat.
